newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW - FNB may shed underperforming units.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - FNB may shed underperforming units.

text.p: South Africa's First National Bank Holdings Ltd (FNB) said on Wednesday it may shed underperforming operations in the 1996/97 financial year, after a year of surging bad debts and a squeeze on margins.

Alec Grant, general manager of public affairs, told Reuters FNB's new managing director Viv Bartlett had made a commitment to raising the bank to international cost-to-income standards within four years.
"He (Bartlett) has committed the FNB group to having a 60 percent non-interest cost to total income ratio," Grant said after the release of FNB's 1995/96 annual results.
"He will not continue with areas that do not meet their 'hurdle rates' over time. So there is a willingness to shed parts of our operation that don't perform," he said.
Hurdle rates were the group's requirements for each operation's net income, return on assets and return on equity.
FNB on Tuesday announced a meagre eight percent rise in headline earnings to 229.8 cents a share in the year to September 30, well below analysts expectations of a 17 percent rise.

The bottom line was particularly hard hit by a 69 percent surge in bad debts to 665.2 million. Businesses responsible for the rise, instalment financiers Wesbank and FirstPref, had already tightened their lending entry levels, Grant said.
"The bad debt provision as a percentage of advances kicked up to over one percent in the past year. We are hoping to get it back to 0.75 where it was last year," he said.
On the outlook for interest rates Grant said based on economic fundamentals FNB expected two one percentage point cuts in Bank rate next year, one in April and the other in September.
However, given the uncertainties in the market, FNB's books were neutrally positioned.
"If rates go up we won't be adversely affected, but we won't benefit to the extent if rates come down," he said.

On Tuesday South African money market traders said the rise in short-term trading rates signalled the market was discounting a hike in the key Bank rate, although they were not convinced the central Reserve Bank would move yet.
The Bank rate is currently at 16 percent.
Shares in FNB slipped 15 cents or 0.6 percent to end at 24.95 rand following the results release. Analysts said the market had been expecting poor results but FNB was set for a better year in 1997.
